lesson.title: Kubernetes from Zero, part 3: your local lab with kind, kubectl and kubeconfig
lesson.shortTitle: Your local lab with kind, kubectl and kubeconfig
lesson.description: Install kubectl and kind, compare minikube, k3d and Docker Desktop, run a three-node cluster, and learn how kubeconfig contexts pick a cluster.
lesson.tested: Installed and checksummed kubectl v1.37.2 and kind v0.33.0; ran 1- and 3-node clusters, 10 Nov 2026
lesson.rule: Use kind for a disposable, multi-node lab, and always know your current context before you type a command.

cheatsheet.intro: The four lab tools, how kubeconfig picks a cluster, and the commands from Lesson 3.

boards.title: Four ways to run a learning cluster
boards.hint: every one of them gives you a real API server

rows.name: kind
rows.role: Each node is a container on Docker, Podman or nerdctl, bootstrapped with kubeadm. Several nodes come from a small config file. The version is the node image.

rows.name: minikube
rows.role: A cluster in a VM, a container, or on the host, depending on the driver. It asks for 2 CPUs, 2 GB of memory and 20 GB of disk, and it has an add-on catalogue.
rows.where: A good fit for a VM lab or its add-ons.

rows.name: k3d
rows.role: Runs k3s in Docker. k3s is a lightweight, fully compliant Kubernetes in a single binary under 100 MB. k3d is a community project, not an official Rancher product.

rows.name: Docker Desktop
rows.role: A built-in cluster: kubeadm (one node, version set by Docker Desktop) or kind (several nodes, version of your choice). Check the licence. Personal, education, non-commercial open source and small businesses are free.
rows.where: Professional use in larger organizations, and government entities, need a paid subscription.

boards.title: kubeconfig
boards.hint: clusters, users, contexts, and one pointer

rows.name: clusters
rows.role: A name, the API server address (`server`), and the certificate authority used to trust it.
rows.where: kind fills this in for you.

rows.name: users
rows.role: A name and the credentials. For kind, a client certificate and key.
rows.where: In clouds this is usually a token plugin.

rows.name: contexts
rows.role: A name that joins one cluster, one user, and an optional default namespace.

rows.name: current-context
rows.role: The context kubectl uses when you do not pass `--context`.

boards.note: Lookup order: the `--kubeconfig` flag if you pass one, otherwise the files in `KUBECONFIG` (colon-separated on Linux and macOS, semicolon on Windows), otherwise `$HOME/.kube/config`. When files are merged, the first file to set a value wins. A kubeconfig is a credential: `chmod 600`, and read an unknown file the way you would read a shell script.

steps.title: What the lab showed
steps.hint: ports, IDs and timings differ on your machine

items.what: `kubectl: OK` and `kind: OK` mean the binary matches the published checksum. The lesson's client is kubectl v1.37.2 and kind v0.33.0. If you see `FAILED`, download both files again.
`kind create cluster --name first` sets the context to `kind-first`. `NotReady` right after creation is normal. A few seconds later the node is `Ready`. kind prefixes the cluster name with `kind-`.

`kind-lab.yaml` asks for one control-plane and two workers. The lesson's nodes are `lab-control-plane`, `lab-worker` and `lab-worker2`, Kubernetes v1.37.0. Only the control-plane containers publish port 6443.

`use-context` changes the kubeconfig. `--context` targets one command. `--minify` shows only the current context and hides certificate data unless you add `--raw`. `set-context --current --namespace` sets the default namespace for commands that omit `-n`.

steps.note: With `KUBECONFIG` listing several files, the first file's `current-context` wins. `kind delete cluster` also removes that cluster's context. Deleting a cluster that does not exist is not an error. For the rest of the series, keep `kind create cluster --name k8s-from-zero`.

homework.intro: Use Docker (or Podman) and the install steps from the lesson. Cluster names, ports and timings will differ. Answers are in the separate answer key.

sections.title: Recall
sections.hint: Answer from memory, then check the lesson.

exercises.q: In one sentence each, how do kind, minikube, k3d and Docker Desktop run a learning cluster?
exercises.a: kind runs each node as a container and bootstraps it with kubeadm. minikube runs a cluster in a VM, a container, or on the host, depending on the driver. k3d runs k3s in Docker. Docker Desktop has a kubeadm mode (one node) and a kind mode (several nodes).

exercises.q: What does the version skew policy say about kubectl and the API server? Which servers does kubectl 1.37 work with?
exercises.a: kubectl is supported within one minor version, older or newer, of the API server. kubectl 1.37 works with API servers 1.36, 1.37 and 1.38.

exercises.q: Name the three lists and the one pointer in a kubeconfig file.
exercises.a: `clusters` (name, server, certificate authority), `users` (name and credentials), `contexts` (one cluster, one user, optional namespace), and `current-context`.

exercises.q: In what order does kubectl pick its configuration file?
exercises.a: The `--kubeconfig` flag if you pass one, otherwise the files listed in `KUBECONFIG`, otherwise `$HOME/.kube/config`. When files are merged, the first file to set a value wins.

exercises.q: Give the two safety notes the lesson gives for a kubeconfig file.
exercises.a: A kubeconfig is a credential: anyone with your kind file is admin on that cluster, so keep it private (`chmod 600`). Use kubeconfig files only from trusted sources, because a crafted file can run code on your machine.

exercises.q: After the checksum commands, what does `kubectl: OK` mean, and what should you do if you see `FAILED`?
exercises.a: `OK` means the binary matches the published checksum. If you see `FAILED`, download both files again.

exercises.q: Create `first` and run `kubectl get nodes` at once. Why might STATUS be `NotReady`, and what is the context name?
exercises.a: `NotReady` right after creation is normal: the network plugin is still starting. A few seconds later the node is `Ready`. The context is `kind-first`, because kind prefixes the cluster name with `kind-`.

exercises.q: Create `lab` from `kind-lab.yaml` and run `docker ps`. Which containers publish a port, and which port is it?
exercises.a: Only the control-plane containers publish a port: the API server's 6443, mapped to a random port on `127.0.0.1`. The lesson's output shows that for `lab-control-plane` and `first-control-plane`.

exercises.q: Run `kubectl config get-contexts`, then `kubectl config use-context kind-first`, then `kubectl get nodes --context kind-lab`. What does the star mean, and which command changes the file?
exercises.a: The star marks the current context. `use-context` changes the kubeconfig file. `--context` targets one command and leaves `current-context` as it was.

exercises.q: Run `kubectl config view --minify`. What does `--minify` leave out, and what would `--raw` add?
exercises.a: `--minify` shows only what the current context uses. Certificate data is `DATA+OMITTED`. `--raw` would print the keys, so the lesson says the command without `--raw` is safe to paste into a ticket.

exercises.q: Point the current context at `kube-system`, list Pods, then set the namespace back to `default`. What changes?
exercises.a: Commands without `-n` go to the context's namespace. With `kube-system`, `kubectl get pods` lists that namespace (CoreDNS, the scheduler, and the rest). Set back to `default`, the lesson prints `No resources found in default namespace`.

exercises.q: Write each cluster's kubeconfig to its own file and run `KUBECONFIG=first.kubeconfig:lab.kubeconfig kubectl config get-contexts`. Which context is current, and why?
exercises.a: The first file set `current-context`, so it wins. In the lesson that is `kind-first`.

sections.title: Predict the outcome
sections.hint: Write your prediction first. Then check the answer key.

exercises.q: You run `kubectl` against the saved `lab.kubeconfig` after `kind delete cluster --name lab`. The error names `127.0.0.1:46163`. What does the lesson say that means?
exercises.a: kubectl points at a cluster that is not running, usually a kubeconfig file or context that outlived its cluster. Check `kubectl config current-context`, then switch context or recreate the cluster.

exercises.q: After both clusters are deleted, kubectl says `The connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused`. Why port 8080?
exercises.a: kubectl found no current context at all, so it fell back to `localhost:8080`. `kubectl config current-context` says `error: current-context is not set`. Create a cluster, or run `kubectl config use-context <name>`.

exercises.q: A three-node create stops at `Preparing nodes` and mentions `could not find a log line that matches "Reached target .*Multi-User System.*|detected cgroup v1"`. What limit is too low, and which commands does the lesson show?
exercises.a: Linux limits on inotify instances and watches. On Ubuntu the defaults are 128 and 8192. The lesson raises them with `sudo sysctl fs.inotify.max_user_instances=512` and `sudo sysctl fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288`, then you create the cluster again.

exercises.q: `kubectl version` shows a client more than one minor version away from the server. What does the lesson say to do?
exercises.a: Some commands may misbehave. Install a kubectl that matches, per the version skew policy.
